title: Dying for the world being born: the education of Emersonian perfectionism
text_snippet: Dying for the world being born: the education of Emersonian perfectionism Abstract This essay argues that Stanley Cavell's philosophy of Emersonian perfectionism amounts to a reconceptualization of education, one responsive to the challenge of each individual living a whole life. In response to our sense that conventional school learning can be alienating and dispiriting, this philosophy opens up a way for us to appreciate the education we may receive from our true friends. Their conversation can lead us each back to the adventure of being born. Such a conception of education, however, calls out to be balanced by a corresponding appreciation of our mortality. Accordingly, my essay also explores how Cavell's thinking may be supplemented by György Lukács's philosophical reflections on the meaning of tragic fate.

title: Consent, harm, and the formation of moral judgement in sex education
text_snippet: Consent, harm, and the formation of moral judgement in sex education Abstract This article re-examines the normative status of consent in sex education by bringing into dialogue two contrasting positions: the mutuality framework proposed by Lamb, Gable, and de Ruyter and Hand’s justificatory account. The central issue is not whether consent is necessary, but which moral standards educators may legitimately promote directively. While Lamb et al. propose mutuality to address interpersonal disregard within consensual acts, Hand maintains that schools may only teach robustly justified standards, specifically consent, harm-avoidance, and promise-keeping. This article accepts Hand’s justificatory restraint but addresses a prior educational question: how individuals acquire the practical judgement required to recognize the circumstances in which justified standards apply. Drawing on philosophical accounts of embodiment and attention, it argues that applying such standards depends upon an ability to perceive possible harms, relevant interests, and commitments within particular encounters. title: Moral education, moral standards, and the moral fixed points
text_snippet: Moral education, moral standards, and the moral fixed points Abstract One thing the moral educator does is to bring people to subscribe to moral standards—that is, norms that purport to reflect morality’s requirements. So a theory of moral education must answer the moral standards question—that is to say, it must incorporate an account of what a moral standard is. The following three claims about the moral standards question are defended in this article. First, the moral standards question is an important choice point in theorizing about moral education that bears significantly on both the theory and practice of moral education. Second, there is reason to reject an influential recent answer to the moral standards question, given by Michael Hand, according to which to subscribe to a moral standard is simply to subscribe to any standard but in a particular way—in Hand’s phrase, to ‘morally subscribe to a standard’. Third, reflection on the defects of Hand’s ‘moral subscription to a standard’ account points towards a promising alternative account of what it is to subscribe to a moral standard—the ‘moral fixed points’ account—which identifies the moral standards by their distinctive content.

title: Unravelling reason: John Stuart Mill and the Education of the Whole Person
text_snippet: Unravelling reason: John Stuart Mill and the Education of the Whole Person Abstract John Stuart Mill would appear to be a natural ally of contemporary appeals to educating the whole person. His critique of one-sided intellectual training and his reflection on feelings and the importance of their cultivation seem to support holistic approaches that oppose narrowly rational and instrumental models of education. Yet this article argues that such readings flatten the significance of Mill’s example and mischaracterize the nature of educational harm that his own life example both reveals and addresses. More specifically, the article argues the central problem of Mill’s early education is not simply that it foregrounded reason and analysis at the expense of feeling, but the way it blocked expressiveness and, with it, possibilities of intelligibility. To make its case, the article will draw upon lines of thinking from Stanley Cavell, particularly his account of the expressiveness of language. It will undertake a close reading of certain passages from Mill’s Autobiography—from which accounts of his one-sided education are often drawn—to examine the work of rendering oneself legible in words. title: Rethinking the idea of the whole person in education
text_snippet: Rethinking the idea of the whole person in education Abstract Against the prevailing instrumentalization and outcomes-based education, there is a resurgence of claims for a holistic conception of education. What does it mean to see a person as a whole—without succumbing to assimilation into the whole or falling into any hardened dichotomy of the inner and the outer? Is there no way of avoiding a withdrawal into subjective innerness and doing justice to inner meaning while at the same time opening ourselves to the public and to the world? In response to these questions, this article will explore an alternative sense of the holistic through a reading of American transcendentalism. As an illustration of a certain mode of suppression disclosed in holistic education, I shall first examine John Miller’s appropriation of American transcendentalism in the scheme of holistic education. Second, in search of a different conception of the holistic and its significance for education, I shall examine Cavell’s reading of the American transcendentalism of Thoreau and show how his reading radically differs from Miller’s. title: Roger T. Ames on Human Becomings and Moral Education: in Conversation with Qasir Shah
text_snippet: Roger T. Ames on Human Becomings and Moral Education: in Conversation with Qasir Shah Abstract Roger T. Ames is a leading contemporary interpreter of Confucian philosophy and a central figure in the development of Confucian role ethics. He is Professor Emeritus of Philosophy at the University of Hawai‘i and currently teaches Chinese philosophy at Peking University (PKU). His work spans comparative philosophy, classical Chinese thought, pragmatism, Daoist and Confucian philosophy, and philosophy of education, with a sustained focus on relational personhood, moral cultivation, and the transformation of experience. In this interview, Ames reflects on education as the lifelong formation of the whole person, rather than as the acquisition of discrete skills or outcomes narrowly defined by institutional metrics. Drawing on Confucian philosophy, pragmatism, and his own pedagogical experience, he presents education as a transformative, relational process grounded in habitude and example. title: Unsettling perfection: the whole person as an end-in-view
text_snippet: Unsettling perfection: the whole person as an end-in-view Abstract Despite its apparent clarity, the notion of a whole person is deeply polysemic, and covers somewhat contradictory conceptions of the specific purpose education should fulfil. Following Paul Standish, this article distinguishes five main models of wholeness (conformist, essentialist, engineered, peregrine, liberal-individualist), and examines how the idea of an education of the whole person could retain its original progressive value. Through a close reading of Philip Roth’s American Pastoral (1997), wholeness as perfection is discussed in its various dimensions, and dismissed for its problematic consequences. Finally, wholeness as an end-in-view, aiming at sociality, is defended as a more desirable and viable alternative.

title: Trust as an ecology: relational, institutional, and systemic conditions in precarious higher education
text_snippet: Trust as an ecology: relational, institutional, and systemic conditions in precarious higher education Abstract Overlapping crises increasingly shape trust in higher education (HE): metric-driven governance, funding volatility, and pervasive precarity among staff and students. This article asks what it means to trust and to be trustworthy within the precarious ecosystem of English HE. Drawing on Baier’s ethics of accepted vulnerability, O’Neill’s conception of institutional trustworthiness, Fricker’s account of epistemic injustice, and Biesta’s world-centred education, this article develops an ecological framework of trust that operates across relational, institutional, and systemic levels. Short vignettes show how trust is enacted or eroded in everyday academic practice, revealing the moral and epistemic labour the university depends on. The analysis shows that breaches of trust at any level reverberate across the wider ecology, exposing the fragility of HE’s moral infrastructure under neoliberal conditions. Reclaiming trust, I argue, requires a reflexive, world-centred commitment to recognition, responsibility, and moral courage. title: Beyond technical competence: reconceptualizing AI literacy through critical pedagogy
text_snippet: Beyond technical competence: reconceptualizing AI literacy through critical pedagogy Abstract This article reconceptualizes AI literacy as conscientização rather than as competency. Existing AI literacy frameworks—such as UNESCO’s policy programme, the AI4K12 curriculum, the influential taxonomy of Long and Magerko, as well as their additive critical extensions—share an architectural commitment that positions critique as one capacity alongside others rather than as the orientation from which AI literacy itself emerges. Drawing on Paulo Freire’s critical pedagogy, John Dewey’s reflective public, feminist standpoint epistemology, and contemporary critical algorithm studies, I propose a constitutive alternative: AI literacy as the development of critical consciousness about socio-technical power, organized through three interrelated dimensions—epistemic reflexivity, political agency, and relational autonomy. These dimensions, which resonate with the philosophical work of Biesta, Stiegler, and Mackenzie, are not three modules of a curriculum, but three faces of one critical consciousness adequate to the algorithmic conjuncture. title: Transitional justice and human flourishing: experiences of victims overcoming large-scale harms as a reference point for school moral education
text_snippet: Transitional justice and human flourishing: experiences of victims overcoming large-scale harms as a reference point for school moral education Abstract This analysis aims to demonstrate how the experiences of victims of large-scale conflicts and injustices—particularly those from societies attempting to implement transitional justice—can contribute to moral education. Its reference point is the concept of human flourishing, understood as development involving the acquisition of moral virtues. By analysing the experiences of victims striving to overcome the consequences of injustice and suffering, a foundation can be established for the development of virtues such as justice, forgiveness, truth-telling, responsibility, and self-education. Through reflection on these experiences, individuals can recognize often difficult to perceive aspects of decision-making in the face of suffering, injustice, and wrongdoing. Considering these when making decisions can protect against falling into traps that lead to the development of moral vices such as vindictiveness, harshness, over-leniency, concealing truth, revealing secrets, and indifference. The experiences of victims in societies marked by conflict and injustice confirm that the boundaries between actions leading to the development of virtues and moral vices are very thin.

title: ‘Boys don’t read that’: lecturers’ perspectives on masculinities and gendered reading cultures in a South African university

Drawing on lecturers’ interpretations, rather than on direct student accounts, this article examines how masculinities are perceived to shape male students’ engagement with gender-sensitive literary texts. Data were generated through semi-structured interviews with six purposively selected English lecturers at a university in the Eastern Cape Province. Thematic analysis revealed lecturers’ recurring observations of avoidance strategies, defensive reading practices, and identity-protective performances of masculinity. title: Beautiful transience. The pedagogical sublation of death in Japanese tea ceremony
text_snippet: Beautiful transience. The pedagogical sublation of death in Japanese tea ceremony Abstract Half a millennium ago, the originally Chinese civilized pastime of drinking tea took on a new form in Japan: influenced by the philosophical practices of Zen Buddhism, it evolved into an art form and one of the ‘paths’ (道 dō) that is meant to help practitioners to obtain a higher awareness of life and to appreciate its transient nature. In this way, the search for meaning took on a new form: not through remembrance of finitude and mortality—that is, the memento mori of the Classic European tradition—did living gain value and worth, but through understanding the value of each moment of life unfolding; instead of propagating a living towards the end, tea ceremony questioned the very idea of time that underlies such strategies of coping. The following argument will outline and analyse the practice of tea ceremony as established by Sen no Rikyū 千利休 (1522–1591) from a pedagogical perspective. title: Learning to die: a response to René Arcilla
text_snippet: Learning to die: a response to René Arcilla Abstract René Arcilla’s ‘Dying for the World Being Born: The Education of Emersonian Perfectionism’ provides an eloquent attempt to address questions regarding the significance of Emersonian moral perfectionism in education and the relation of the tragic dimension of human experience to this. He leads the reader into difficult territory, powerfully evoking dimensions of human experience that educational institutions for the most part set aside. The moving account of his own experience and the part that philosophy played in it lays the way for a questioning of the extent to which a sense of the tragic plays a part in education, thematizing the dying and being born in his title. My discussion acknowledges a degree of unease regarding thematizations of death and rebirth. title: What should educators do about bad beliefs?
text_snippet: What should educators do about bad beliefs? Abstract Bad beliefs are beliefs that are contrary to settled expert opinion; beliefs like ‘global warming is a myth’ or ‘vaccines cause autism’. Non-experts should defer to experts when they are not themselves able to assess the evidence, so we should reject bad beliefs. Notoriously, though, large numbers of people report believing these things, and even more bizarre assertions. Many philosophers think we can avoid bad beliefs by teaching critical thinking or inculcating virtues. While these strategies have some effect, I am sceptical that they achieve very much. In fact, most people—including those who accept bad beliefs—are already broadly rational and believe what they have most reason to believe. I argue that educators do better to tackle the problem indirectly: by acknowledging the rationality of bad believers and by being realistic about what we can know and about how knowledge is produced.

title: In the wake of wholeness: education, ethics, and the Confucian self
text_snippet: In the wake of wholeness: education, ethics, and the Confucian self Abstract This paper critically re-examines the ideal of educating the ‘whole person’ in light of contemporary social, moral, and ecological crises. While holistic education has gained renewed prominence, such approaches often rely on perfectionist or reductive models that suppress ambiguity, vulnerability, and relational complexity. Engaging with Paul Standish’s postmodern critique, the paper contends that appeals to wholeness risk imposing closure where ethical openness is required. In response, it turns to Confucian philosophy—both classical and contemporary—as a resource for reimagining moral education. At the heart of this alternative is the jūnzǐ (君子), or exemplary person, whose character is formed not through completion but through continuous ethical cultivation within a web of relationships. This process is guided by the Five Constant Virtues: rén (co-humanity), yì (appropriateness), lǐ (ritual propriety), zhì (wisdom), and xìn (making good on one’s word), as well as by chéng (誠), a dynamic sincerity that binds intention and action across shifting contexts. title: Ecointelligence and the future of education: a philosophical framework for human–machine symbiosis
text_snippet: Ecointelligence and the future of education: a philosophical framework for human–machine symbiosis Abstract The infiltration of intelligent reasoning systems into human cognition necessitates a paradigm shift in education away from cultivating individual minds and towards constructing ‘distributed ecointelligence’. Grounded in the Extended Mind Theory and evolutionary epistemology, this article develops a primarily epistemological framework for understanding technology-mediated cognition and its implications for education. It introduces ‘ecointelligence’ as a conceptual model that captures the co-evolution of human cognition, technological mediation, and contextual environments. While the analysis is fundamentally theoretical, it outlines certain pedagogical implications for rethinking learning, teaching, and assessment in artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated environments. By examining the philosophical evolution of cognitive tools, the dilemmas of technological mediation, and pathways for educational transformation, this article argues that future education must prioritize a dynamic balance between mental subjectivity and technological empowerment. title: From the Kyoto School to a pragmatic philosophy of awakening
text_snippet: From the Kyoto School to a pragmatic philosophy of awakening Abstract The purpose of this article is to examine the education of the whole person from the Kyoto School of Philosophy founder Nishida Kitarō’s (1932) ‘On Education’ as compared with John Dewey’s pragmatism. Using the Kyoto School pragmatist Mori Akira as a mediator, this article examines three facets of the issue: the non-dual starting point of education between abstract materialism and idealism, the fundamentally relational nature of the person, and the creative formation of history. This analysis reveals tensions between Nishida and Dewey with regard to learning from consequences and existential self-awareness. This article concludes with an attempt at a pragmatic philosophy of awakening, demonstrating the value of combining these views and thus addressing the criticism that the ‘holistic education’ of the Kyoto School is developmentalist and mystical.

In empirical conditions, for instance, in school systems characterized by segregation and inequalities, citizenship education should develop both PL and CL. title: Scholè as suspension: a political project?
text_snippet: Scholè as suspension: a political project? Abstract In this article, we explore the notion of scholè as suspension, central to Jan Masschelein and Maarten Simon’s work on the publicness of school, with the aim of addressing the position that scholè as suspension can be conceptualized as non-political. We begin by discussing Masschelein and Simons’ idea. Further, we suggest a contrast with the understanding of suspension put forward in Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s Émile, ou de l’éducation. This alternative account challenges the centrality of schools in enabling suspension and shows that embracing the school as the pre-eminent site of the scholè can run the risk of perpetuating injustice. title: Philosophy is not a ‘blood sport’: education as a pathway towards developing a more generous, communal mode of philosophizing
text_snippet: Philosophy is not a ‘blood sport’: education as a pathway towards developing a more generous, communal mode of philosophizing Abstract Norman Swartz’s 1994 essay, ‘Is Philosophy a Blood Sport?’, provides the starting point for this article which explores ways—especially educational ones—of developing a more communal and generous mode of philosophizing. The article is motivated by a desire to prevent the potential corruption of philosophy by tempering the influence of competition and combativeness that threaten to turn it into a ‘blood sport’. To this end, I hope to develop pathways by which to return philosophy to a certain conception of its proper objective: namely, the pursuit of greater world-understanding and wisdom. This more generous, more communal approach nevertheless does not shy away from disagreement, critique, and challenging conversations. By encouraging and facilitating insightful dialogue, it allows for the realization of philosophical potential. Through an exploration of the philosophy of Friedrich Nietzsche, Rosalyn Diprose, and Maurice Merleau-Ponty, the article demonstrates the creative potential of corporeality, affect, and engagements with other people in the philosophical transformation of meaning. title: The argument from justified curriculum development for teaching philosophy in primary schools
text_snippet: The argument from justified curriculum development for teaching philosophy in primary schools Abstract This article offers a novel argument in favour of teaching philosophy as a compulsory subject from primary school onwards, the argument from justified curriculum development. The argument from justified curriculum development identifies a comprehensive set of crucial normative problems that compose the problem of selecting the goals and content of school curricula and that are crucial for determining the justificatory status of obeying various norms. title: On the meeting of minds
text_snippet: On the meeting of minds Abstract This article explores the notion of the meeting of minds. I give content to the notion, first by removing philosophical obstacles that prevent us from making good sense of the idea, and then by exploring various possibilities: directly discerning what someone is thinking or feeling; learning what they think or feel by hearing what they say; apprehending the same thought; harmony in intelligent action; thinking or acting together in reciprocal recognition of a shared endeavour; and mutually established like-mindedness, serving as the background to moral, practical, or theoretical pursuits. In this, I move from the idea of apprehending or perceiving other minds, through the idea of shared acts of reason, to the concept of shared ethos, and thus from an appreciation of particular episodes in which minds meet to the idea of a mutual affinity of perception and response that can endure notwithstanding the possibility of disagreement. The article draws on Cavell, Frege, Köhler, McDowell, Wiggins, and Wittgenstein, among others, to explore the philosophical and educational implications of these ideas.

title: When inclusion excludes: liberalism, Confucianism, and the Parkfield Community School protests
text_snippet: When inclusion excludes: liberalism, Confucianism, and the Parkfield Community School protests Abstract This article examines the 2019 Parkfield Community School protests in Birmingham as a case-based philosophical analysis in the moral and relational limits of liberal inclusion within public education. It critically engages Abeera Khan’s analysis of securitized liberalism, which shows how Muslim parental dissent was pathologized and rendered unintelligible within dominant civic discourses. At the same time, it draws on Nora Hämäläinen’s model of moral renegotiation, which highlights the affective and temporal complexities of ethical disagreement. While Hämäläinen offers a compelling alternative to procedural liberalism, her framework still presumes the presence of discursive and affective equality—conditions that were structurally absent at Parkfield. To respond to this gap, the article turns to Confucian relational ethics, proposing that virtues such as rén (consummate conduct), chéng (sincerity), and xìn (making good on one’s word) offer a deeper account of the cultivated moral capacities necessary for enduring disagreement. title: Decolonizing philosophy of education: in the shadow of the Enlightenment?
text_snippet: Decolonizing philosophy of education: in the shadow of the Enlightenment? Abstract The imperative to decolonize—usually targeted on decolonizing the curriculum in schools and universities—has become a prominent focus in philosophy of education. Welcoming the overdue anti-colonial turn, in this article we ask what is demanded of a decolonized philosophy of education. With Western philosophy under review, we focus on the Enlightenment—a primary target, especially of decolonial theorists, for critique in addressing Empire and its afterlife. Noting how it is commonly regarded as interchangeable with Western thought and modernity, we assess decolonial depictions of the Enlightenment as complicit in colonialism and show that there is a tendency to homogenize it as a unified project with a singular agenda. Philosophers of education exploring the implications of calls for decolonization of the discipline may feel compelled by such critiques to repudiate the Enlightenment entirely. With particular reference to the discipline in Britain, given its colonial past and elements of coloniality that persist, our own stance on whether there could be a role for the Enlightenment in philosophy of education in a time of decolonization is a qualified ‘yes’.

title: Why do we teach?
text_snippet: Why do we teach? Abstract The ubiquity of teaching in human societies presents a significant puzzle, particularly considering that much of modern education involves abstract concepts which do not directly enhance survival. This article reviews two main perspectives on the origins of teaching: teaching as a cognitive adaptation for transmitting complex knowledge, and teaching as a cultural product of modern societies. The evidence indicates that teaching is present in all societies, suggesting it may be an evolutionary adaptation. However, skills, including complex ones, can be acquired through other forms of social learning such as imitation. This article proposes a third perspective: teaching as a by-product of our proclivity to cooperate. By examining ethnographic studies, psychology experiments, and surveys on teachers’ motivations, this article argues that teaching requires traits like mind-reading, communication, and altruism, which are foundational for cooperation. Teaching reflects our social nature, and is not just a mechanism for knowledge transmission. title: Epistemic authenticity in liberal education and the value of coming to own one’s beliefs
text_snippet: Epistemic authenticity in liberal education and the value of coming to own one’s beliefs Abstract I propose a notion of teaching for epistemic authenticity which involves providing students with knowledge about a range of choices on how to live a flourishing life and encouraging students to reflect critically on their own belief commitments and external influences on their beliefs. I suggest that this notion of teaching about diverse ways of living broadens moral education acquired at home and is justified under both perfectionist and anti-perfectionist strands of liberalism even in cases when parents disagree with such teaching. I then turn to the notion of indoctrination, and argue that when instruction conducive to epistemic authenticity in schools with liberal tradition is taught through critical discourse, such instruction is not indoctrinating, but rather a means of fostering informed and independent thinking, thereby empowering students to make autonomous decisions about their beliefs.

title: On the distribution of labour(s) in reckoning with hard histories
text_snippet: On the distribution of labour(s) in reckoning with hard histories Abstract This article explores the ethical distribution of labour in addressing ‘hard history’ within cultural communities, focusing on histories that are difficult to confront due to their complex and emotionally charged nature. These include events like the genocide of Indigenous populations in the USA and the impacts of colonialism in the UK. Hard histories challenge national narratives and cultural identities; they evoke strong emotional responses, necessitating a deeper understanding of the past and its present implications. The central argument of the article is that, within a community, the responsibility for engaging with hard histories should not (as it often does) disproportionately fall on those who have been most directly harmed. title: Philosophy as a way of life for children: towards a transformative educational ethos
text_snippet: Philosophy as a way of life for children: towards a transformative educational ethos Abstract This article argues that philosophy, when approached as a lived, dialogical, and inclusive practice, can and should be a way of life for children. Drawing on the Philosophy for Children (P4C) movement, the article challenges assumptions that philosophical enquiry is too abstract or advanced for young learners. It explores how diverse philosophical traditions, including Dewey’s pragmatism, Buber’s dialogical ethics, Kant’s constructivist epistemology, Wittgenstein’s language games, and Heidegger’s existential questioning, affirm children’s capacity for philosophical engagement. The article further draws on developmental psychology and pragmatist ethics to show how children think critically, reason ethically, and contribute meaningfully to philosophical dialogue. By foregrounding children as capable thinkers, the article reimagines education as a transformative ethos rooted in enquiry, reflection, and shared meaning-making. P4C is presented not simply as a pedagogy, but as a democratic, humanistic practice that affirms children’s full participation in intellectual and moral life.

title: The freedom to be bad: exploring teacher–student conflict and the possibility for education as subjectification
text_snippet: The freedom to be bad: exploring teacher–student conflict and the possibility for education as subjectification Abstract This article is an effort to explore an incident of conflict that occurred between me—as a teacher in a private tutoring agency—and a fourth-grade boy, Jie, who was under my supervision. During this incident, Jie uttered a physical threat which he directed towards me after I nagged him about his disruptive behaviours. In response, I gave Jie permission to carry out his threat of physical violence against me, but he refrained from doing so. After the incident, we developed a somewhat positive relationship, with Jie showing significant improvement in his conduct. I do not refer to this incident as an example of ‘what to do in a situation like this’, but rather to explore various possible interpretations of the event from a philosophical and educational point of view. In this article, I first discuss two key themes relevant to this incident—namely, freedom and ‘being bad’—and their relationship to one another, before providing a description of the incident itself. I then present the interpretation of the incident that constituted my initial understanding of ‘why my method worked’. I then problematize this interpretation and offer three alternatives, discussing their viability

title: Teaching the web of rationality: a case study on coherence and conspiracy world-views
text_snippet: Teaching the web of rationality: a case study on coherence and conspiracy world-views Abstract In this article, we analyse how coherence should be addressed in critical thinking courses. Our starting point is the fact that, while coherence seems important for rationality and critical thinking, several studies now suggest that thinkers with conspiracy world-views give more importance to coherence than other criteria. However, conspiracy world-views do not (fully) embrace the ideals of rationality and critical thinking. This suggests that some desiderata of rationality or critical thinking can, in isolation, be counterproductive. In response to this puzzle, we first argue that coherence cannot be separated from other desiderata of critical thinking. Becoming more coherent does not necessarily matter if one is unresponsive to the evidence, fails to reason on the basis of justified attitudes, and so forth. Then, we turn to consider the concrete actions that can be implemented in critical thinking courses which would reflect this. Articulating the relationships between the various desiderata of rationality can be difficult in introductory critical thinking courses, since they usually carry different objectives. title: ‘What they have made of us’: the educational experience of Bildung in vocational education
text_snippet: ‘What they have made of us’: the educational experience of Bildung in vocational education Abstract This article explores the role of Bildung in vocational education, questioning whether it can effectively create the values it aims to instil. While Bildung has traditionally been seen as separate from vocational training, recent discussions in the Netherlands have sought to integrate it into post secondary vocational education (middelbaar beroepsonderwijs or mbo). However, Bildung relies on implicit assumptions about how students attribute meaning to their education, which risks undermining its own ideals. To address this issue, the article argues that Bildung must become part of the students’ process of self-formation rather than a predefined educational goal. The argument unfolds in three steps. First, the historical and political roots of Bildung in vocational education are examined, revealing its dual function: fostering individual freedom while also shaping good citizenship and vocational identity. This duality exposes Bildung to the critique of elitism. Second, Wolfgang Klafki’s concept of Allgemeinbildung is analysed for its potential to address this critique, but it is found to tacitly impose predetermined values on students. title: Against teaching propositional belief in higher education and the World Religions Paradigm
text_snippet: Against teaching propositional belief in higher education and the World Religions Paradigm Abstract This article outlines some problems inherent in the World Religions Paradigm and focuses on the problem of teaching propositional belief. By comparing belief to faith, this article suggests that teaching World Religions in higher education can be done without propositional belief and through a practice-oriented alternative. Using one line of thought in the philosophy of education, this article argues that teachers can adjust the World Religions Paradigm, rather than getting rid of it all together. This adjustment is based on Wrathall’s neo-Heideggerian argument that praxis-oriented faith and lived religious experience should be fundamental to World Religions in higher education.

title: ‘Covert no-saying’: a framework for democratic education in illiberal democracies
text_snippet: ‘Covert no-saying’: a framework for democratic education in illiberal democracies Abstract This article develops the concept of ‘covert no-saying’ as a pragmatic framework for democratic education in illiberal democracies. Drawing on pragmatist philosophy, it argues that traditional approaches—‘yes-saying’ (compliance) and ‘drastic no-saying’ (overt dissent)—are increasingly untenable in contexts marked by repression, polarization, and diminishing civil liberties. Instead, educators should foster ‘covert no-saying’: indirect, strategic forms of dissent that preserve democratic values while minimizing personal and professional risk. Through analysis of classroom strategies such as coded language, allegory, comparative case studies, and critical media literacy, the article illustrates how teachers can nurture critical reflection and resilience in students without openly confronting illiberal authorities. The discussion highlights the importance of adaptive teacher education and collaborative support networks for sustaining democratic practice under adverse conditions. Ultimately, the article contends that covert no-saying offers a vital, context-sensitive response to democratic backsliding, enabling educators and students alike to maintain hope and agency in the o

title: Between the categorial and the normative: challenges within contemporary analytic philosophy of education
text_snippet: Between the categorial and the normative: challenges within contemporary analytic philosophy of education Abstract This article raises the question as to whether philosophy of education has both categorial and normative commitments, and argues that it has both. First, it discusses categorial philosophy of education (CPED) in terms of two possible forms: one which involves uncontroversial anthropological considerations, and one which makes substantial claims about human nature. Each is framed with examples. Normative philosophy of education (NPED) is then introduced and contrasted with the categorial version. An illustrative example from Rousseau demonstrates the close relationship between normative political philosophy and NPED. The article then presents an extended example of NPED, relating this to contemporary discussions of conceptual engineering. The work of R. S. Peters is considered as a sustained and partly successful attempt to disentangle categorial and normative elements in his own evolving philosophy of education. Finally, the relationship between CPED and NPED is outlined.

title: Back to Socrates: on the significance of analogue pedagogy in the age of content
text_snippet: Back to Socrates: on the significance of analogue pedagogy in the age of content Abstract The crisis of the digitization of human culture may be the most acute since the agricultural revolution that founded our civilization about ten thousand years ago. Given the tectonic nature of the current civilizational upheaval, it is not surprising that revolutionary transformations are taking place in education and pedagogy as well. Educational institutions increasingly rely on the technological possibilities of digitization in order to enrich or even replace traditional teaching methods. Such remarkable and seemingly effective innovations raise a critical question: which elements of the old world do we want to preserve and sustain in the new one? This article brings insights from Socratic pedagogy to bear on digital education, exploring the ways in which Socrates’ views on education and the limits of written language can assist in our attempts to strike a balance between the innovative technologies that will be integrated into education, and the traditional methods it would be wise to preserve, and perhaps even refine, in light of the Socratic pedagogical legacy. title: Will generative AI ‘change everything’ in education, and if so, how could we know?: assessing neohumanist and posthumanist answers
text_snippet: Will generative AI ‘change everything’ in education, and if so, how could we know?: assessing neohumanist and posthumanist answers Abstract The article starts with the popular diagnosis that generative artificial intelligence (genAI) will ‘change everything’ in education and asks what such a fundamental change would entail—and if we would even notice it under our current theoretical frameworks. It then analyses two such frameworks—namely, Martha Nussbaum’s neohumanist theory and posthumanist theory—to see if they can provide guidance in this potential new situation. Nussbaum’s theory is found to fall short in terms of appreciating the potential positive developments the introduction of genAI could bring, such as the emergence of new capabilities that are not covered by her framework. Posthumanist theory faces the opposite problem—not being good enough at identifying the potentially dangerous outcomes of using genAI in the classroom. The article ends with suggestions concerning a possible path forward, incorporating the most valuable insights of each theory.

title: Euphemia Haynes’ philosophy of mathematics and mathematics education
text_snippet: Euphemia Haynes’ philosophy of mathematics and mathematics education Abstract Euphemia Lofton Haynes was a renowned mathematician and mathematics educator, and notably the first Black American woman to complete a PhD in mathematics, which was not widely known until the late 20th century and early 21st century. Even less well known are her interactions with the philosophy of logic and mathematics. In fact, as evidenced by her academic career, addresses to mathematics educators, and personal testimony, Haynes’ approach to mathematics education was informed by philosophical views that she developed over the course of her life. This article examines the development of Haynes’ views and the manner in which she applied said views in the field of mathematics education. The major themes that develop out of her addresses are a characterization of mathematics as involving abstract thinking, a form of pluralistic constructivism, an opposition to mathematics as mere calculation, and a unique notion of ‘mathematizing life’.

title: Addendum to the Educational Goods Framework: the call for guidance for collective decision-making
text_snippet: Addendum to the Educational Goods Framework: the call for guidance for collective decision-making Abstract This article focuses on the four-step schema introduced by Harry Brighouse, Helen F. Ladd, Susanna Loeb, and Adam Swift for operationalizing the Educational Goods Framework and making ‘value-led and data-informed’ decisions in education. The four steps are (1) identify the main values at play; (2) identify the key decisions relevant to those values; (3) assess the options in light of the values and evidence; and (4) establish what is the best policy overall in the circumstances. In this article, we point out the ambiguities in this four-step approach and argue that its lack of clarity carries the danger of causing ethical problems in certain real-world educational contexts. We demonstrate our points through two cases in El Salvador, a country with non-ideal features that render it challenging to implement Brighouse and Swift’s idealized vision of rational, impartial, and informed decision-making processes. We conclude with a call for adding normative guidance on collective decision-making as an addendum to the Educational Goods Framework and note its potential utility in contexts beyond El Salvador.

title: Can education liberate us? Reframing an old question
text_snippet: Can education liberate us? Reframing an old question Abstract This article reframes the question ‘Can education liberate us?’ by shifting attention from education’s capacity to produce emancipated individuals to its capacity to enable—or foreclose—liberation within the experience of subjectivation. Instead of proposing new educational theory or conducting empirical research, it examines how normative frameworks in educational discourse limit possibilities for thinking about freedom and self-relation. Drawing on Martin Heidegger’s and Michel Foucault’s respective critiques, the article argues that liberation must target not just the individual, but the very experience by which one comes to recognize oneself as an educational subject. Through critical analysis of Paulo Freire, critical pedagogy traditions, and Gert J. J. Biesta’s vision of democratic education, it shows that the most explicitly critical approaches operate within normative frameworks that presuppose specific forms of subjectivity, and predetermine what liberation means. As a counterpoint, the article returns to Plato’s paideia, reinterpreting it through Foucault’s ‘technologies of the self’, and Heidegger’s analysis of the Cave Allegory. title: Between Butes and the digital player: paradoxes of Eros
text_snippet: Between Butes and the digital player: paradoxes of Eros Abstract This article questions the meaning of Eros in sexual desire and education by comparing the Greek mythological figure Butes—who, enchanted by the Sirens’ song, throws himself into the sea despite the risk of death—with today’s narcissistic ‘digital players’, who, through dating apps, AI, or virtual reality, exchange only pleasure while avoiding negativity. First, it examines Pascal Quignard’s Boutès (2008), contrasting Butes with both Orpheus, who neutralizes the Sirens’ song with his own music, and Odysseus, who is bound to the mast to resist the Sirens’ seduction. Through Anne Carson’s Eros the Bittersweet (1986), the article also emphasizes the paradoxical nature of Eros, which inherently involves madness and suffering: it critiques today’s tendency towards convenient love that seeks only controlled, safe thrills with risk-free desire. Furthermore, drawing on Plato’s Symposium and Phaedrus, this article develops Carson’s idea of Eros as the ‘desire to know the unknown’, highlighting the similarities between Eros and knowing, the lover and the thinker. title: Enriching and extending the ecological perspective on teacher agency
text_snippet: Enriching and extending the ecological perspective on teacher agency Abstract Recent concern in the Anglophone-West over teacher autonomy, well-being, demoralization, and retention, as well as increasing strike action, point to a critical moment in the work lives of schoolteachers. In response, scholars have reached for diverse conceptions of teacher agency. I argue that a robust and adequate response to the current crisis requires that teacher agency be tightly coupled with a distinct form of intentionality. At stake here is the intention to educate—to help students discern what goals and intentions are worthwhile. Given this view, what are the conditions of teacher agency? Mark Priestley, Gert Biesta, and Sarah Robinson’s ecological approach to teacher agency offers a viable start; yet it is limited by its adherence to the existing education system bureaucracy. I turn to the enactivist account of agency in order to extend and enrich their ecological account. According to enactivism, agents are driven by the goal of maintaining identity. Intentions are shaped and sustained in response to the agent’s situation. When an intention becomes unsustainable in a given context, agents will pursue other means of self-maintenance. title: Teaching evolution in schools: a thin comprehensive liberal approach
text_snippet: Teaching evolution in schools: a thin comprehensive liberal approach Abstract Comprehensive liberals and political liberals disagree over the extent to which the compulsory school curriculum must be ‘neutral’, in the sense of avoiding taking a stance on value-disagreements between citizens. Problems with these two liberal positions come to the fore when we consider what each has to say about the inclusion of evolutionary theory on the curriculum. Comprehensive liberals have justified its inclusion by appealing to the intrinsic value of this knowledge. But their appeal to controversial justifications is rejected by some as failing to show respect for the free, equal, and rational status of citizens. The majority of political liberals have also supported evolution’s inclusion on the curriculum, offering ‘neutral’ arguments that appeal to the value of scientific understanding. But these arguments face various challenges, including that they do not justify the teaching of evolutionary theory specifically. ‘Thin comprehensive liberalism’ offers a distinctive approach that avoids the main pitfalls of the two dominant positions within liberalism. title: Rethinking contextualization in history education
text_snippet: Rethinking contextualization in history education Abstract This article rethinks contextualization in history education by arguing that it should be viewed not as a domain-specific heuristic but as an ordinary act of human understanding. Drawing on linguistic, ideational, and cultural traditions of contextualism—from Wittgenstein’s ‘meaning as use’ and Austin’s illocutionary acts to Bevir’s webs of belief and Geertz’s ‘thick description’—it demonstrates that contextualization underlies everyday reasoning. Challenging Wineburg’s view of contextualization as an ‘unnatural act’, the article contends that history education should refine rather than replace students’ intuitive contextual reasoning. It further proposes that instruction preceding contextualization should focus on helping students conceptualize the nature of historical context and examine the contingent relationship between past and present. This approach seeks to connect disciplinary historical enquiry with the interpretive capacities that guide ordinary human understanding.

title: The obligation to restrict AI in student writing
text_snippet: The obligation to restrict AI in student writing Abstract The response to student use of generative AI in higher education has been characterized by ambiguity, and no set of policies has yet become the accepted norm. Individual instructors are, so far, able to take wildly divergent approaches. In this article, I address the use of AI to specifically produce text for written assignments, arguing that universities have an obligation to regulate such uses. I argue that, even if using AI for writing is not technically plagiarism, it undermines education in the same way that plagiarism does. For this reason, educators have a moral obligation to treat AI-generated text, in the context of student education, the same way they would treat text written by a person. Given the impact AI text generation is already having on student practice, I argue that universities have a duty to act quickly and decisively to implement preventative measures and common norms restricting the use of AI in written assignments.

title: Not just Émile : exploring the education of new teachers through a Rousseauian lens
text_snippet: Not just Émile : exploring the education of new teachers through a Rousseauian lens Abstract The UK (United Kingdom) government’s evolving strategies for teacher recruitment and statutory guidance have cultivated a dynamic cohort of new teachers with ever-changing needs. Drawing on Rousseau’s educational philosophy, this theoretical article advocates for a personalized and autonomous approach to teacher training. It tentatively introduces the term ‘Émilian Autodidacticism’, inspired by Rousseau’s Émile, or on Education. This article contends that Émilian Autodidacticism, despite its inherent flaws and contradictions, offers a valuable mentoring framework. It places the mentee at the centre of their own learning, fostering autonomy and self-directed growth. By emphasizing the teacher’s active role in their own development, this approach provides a meaningful and personalized mentoring system for new teachers. Additionally, this article aims to bridge theory and practice, presenting Émilian Autodidacticism as an alternative way to support beginning teachers.

title: Decolonizing human rights education, Eurocentrism, and human rights universals
text_snippet: Decolonizing human rights education, Eurocentrism, and human rights universals Abstract Critical reflection on the history, conceptual underpinnings, and practices of human rights education (HRE) has prompted calls for the field to be decolonized, in response to the injustices of colonial history and persisting present-day coloniality. We sympathize with current calls to decolonize and value their effect in prompting critical reflection on Empire in all its facets, yet we also regard HRE as having a credible role to play in response to both colonialism and continuing coloniality. Addressing the decolonial criticism of human rights education as undermined by Western, European, universalist underpinnings, we question its account of European thought. In doing so we distinguish between a qualified universalism on the one hand, which we support, and colonial hypocrisy and pseudo-universalism on the other. Favouring a postcolonial stance, we argue that while the practices of HRE must reflect local diversity, its conceptual foundations are neither historically fixed nor geographically determined. We reflect on the prospects for developing a conceptually coherent and programmatically defensible HRE if we embrace the decolonization imperative’s scepticism about Europe

title: Learning Andy Clark & David Chalmers’ ‘The Extended Mind’ through Christopher Nolan’s Memento
text_snippet: Learning Andy Clark & David Chalmers’ ‘The Extended Mind’ through Christopher Nolan’s Memento Abstract This article presents a case for engaging with fictional narratives to teach philosophical concepts, specifically exploring Christopher Nolan’s Memento to teach concepts related to Andy Clark and David Chalmers’ ‘The Extended Mind Thesis’ (EMT). I contrast a ‘theoretical’ approach to teaching EMT—that is, teaching these concepts by engaging directly with Clark and Chalmers’ text—with an alternative that has students engage with the film. I argue this alternative is preferable in overcoming three barriers to learning that plague the theoretical approach: language, theoretical background, and passivity. I describe how EMT concepts could be taught without engaging with the film, but suggest that if one were to adopt this approach, the concepts would be limited in terms of how they relate to students, their accessibility, and what they ask of them. title: Why not replace people with machines? Exploring Artificial Intelligence’s (in)capacity for education as subjectification
text_snippet: Why not replace people with machines? Exploring Artificial Intelligence’s (in)capacity for education as subjectification Abstract The rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has prompted many professional fields to replace their human workers with AI systems. In the field of education, however, people generally do recognize the many limitations of AI in comparison to human educators. Much of the discussion on AI limitations, however, centres around the more technical and functional shortcomings of the current technology, which could, at least theoretically, be resolved by further technological advancements. The purpose of this article, however, is to point out the fundamental limitations of AI in education so that such a technology could be used more appropriately and responsibly. Building on the conceptualization of education as (at least partly) subjectification through intersubjectivity, which demands both parties involved to be and be treated as subjects, this article argues that there is at least one aspect in which AI (in its current form) could never replace humans as educators: its lack of subject-ness. title: Common sense and critical pedagogy
text_snippet: Common sense and critical pedagogy Abstract This article critically examines the concept of common sense within the context of critical pedagogy, exploring its role as both a potential obstacle and a tool in counter-hegemonic education. Drawing on the work of Wittgenstein, and of theorists such as Dotson and Kumashiro, the article argues that hegemonic common sense constrains educational practices by reinforcing dominant social norms, thus marginalizing alternative forms of knowledge and life. The analysis challenges Carusi’s argument that a counter-hegemonic common sense is not only possible but necessary, suggesting instead that such a common sense is inherently difficult to achieve due to its incommensurability with hegemonic norms. Through a Wittgensteinian lens, the article contends that whilst theory is crucial for the development of counter-hegemonic ideas, the existential and epistemic challenges they present may render them unintelligible within the framework of dominant common sense. This article suggests some possible approaches to ‘counter-hegemonic’ teaching material.

title: The place of remorse in a child’s life
text_snippet: The place of remorse in a child’s life Abstract What kind of moral lessons do children learn when they fight and forgive one another? What happens in the process of reconciliation and apprehending the plight of those they have wronged? In this article, I explore moral education from the point of view of remorse. In line with the vital role learning from mistakes and wrongdoing plays in the educational process of children, I claim that children’s experiences of remorse in response to those they have wronged can pave the way for moral transformation, thereby shaping their character, moral identity, and moral behaviour. I argue that remorse can deepen their moral understanding in ways that they can never imagine for themselves. Drawing on the works of Raimond Gaita and Christopher Cordner, I critically analyse the connection between remorse and inner transformation, and I place this analysis in the context of the moral education of children.

title: Reconsidering ritual in education
text_snippet: Reconsidering ritual in education Abstract Our focus in this article is on the necessity in teacher education and educational research of revisiting ritual as a guiding, limiting practice in our field. First, we spend time with an etymology of ‘ritual’ to account for the ways in which its linguistic history has shifted, and fixed, a sense of what ritual is and might do. Second, we conduct a necessarily partial survey of ritual in the academic literature for the sake of setting the stakes of the term itself, as well as the ways in which it has been developed over time through research, broadly. We narrow, then, to considering ritual through the lens of two primary sources: educational critique, and Foucault. From there, we consider manifestations of ritual as they come to demand certain forms of avowal from educators and educational researchers, occluding access to other modes of enquiry, different stances, and varied possibilities for truths.

title: Reframing inclusion. Analysis of the promises and limitations of Rancière’s work for inclusive education
text_snippet: Reframing inclusion. Analysis of the promises and limitations of Rancière’s work for inclusive education Abstract In inclusion as traditionally understood, those on the inside seek to include those on the outside. Reversing this understanding, the French philosopher Jacques Rancière argues for a notion of inclusion that works from the outside in, with those on the outside including themselves. These ideas stem from Rancière’s central thesis that everybody has an equal capacity to speak and to express their requests. In this article, I develop a concept of inclusive education based on Rancière’s notions of ‘equality’, ‘distribution of the sensible’, and ‘politics’, and analyse whether it justifies a reframing of inclusion or ultimately falls short. After briefly defining inclusive education, I present the key concepts from Rancière’s work necessary to explore a Rancièrean notion of inclusion. I then discuss the promises and, above all, the limitations of adapting Rancière’s political thought to the field of inclusive education. The principal limitation is that, in education, we cannot ignore that some people lack the capacity to express their requests independently. To address this, I turn to the French philosopher Jean-Luc Nancy’s account of equality as the infinite potential of meani

title: Empowering young voices through performing poetry
text_snippet: Empowering young voices through performing poetry Abstract In this article we examine the potential of writing and performing poetry to empower young people from marginalized backgrounds to participate in the political life of their communities. Our method combines philosophical analysis with the design and implementation of a poetry workshop in Coventry. Drawing on Cavell’s notion of ‘acknowledgement’, we begin with a philosophical account of the pedagogy that informed the workshop’s design. We then explore how this account informed implementation of the workshop. Finally, we present the results. To unpack the significance of our findings, we examine two poems performed by young people at the project’s concluding event. On empirical and philosophical grounds, we argue that writing and performing poetry can play a role in political education, for it opens space for what we call ‘the acknowledgement of voice’.

title: Sense and sensibility: Stanley Cavell's philosophy of moral manners
text_snippet: Sense and sensibility: Stanley Cavell's philosophy of moral manners ABSTRACT In this essay, Emily Miller Budick sets out to explore narrative in the manner that it appears in Stanley Cavell's writings, as a way of exploring the human condition. Storytelling can be in service of didactic or moralistic argument or principles. But those dimensions of human experience—in ethics, epistemology, politics, metaphysics—coexist and are co-dependent on human minds that perceive and live these matters. ‘Suppose', Cavell writes in Conditions Handsome and Unhandsome, ‘the issue is not to win an argument, but to manifest for the other another way.' Stories, and critical reflection upon them, can open the possibility of other ways of thinking and other ways of being. In the light of references to Jane Austen and to Emerson's ‘aversion to conformity', the essay reflects on aspects of Cavell's autobiographical writings, especially on the significance of his recollections of his friend, the philosopher Kurt Fischer. It goes on to focus on questions of race and antisemitism, in the light of close attention to J. M. Coetzee’s novels, Disgrace and Elizabeth Costello.

title: ‘The wild-goose is more of a cosmopolite than we’: encountering the untranslatable, becoming cosmopolitan
text_snippet: ‘The wild-goose is more of a cosmopolite than we’: encountering the untranslatable, becoming cosmopolitan Abstract Taking Dewey's cosmopolitan call as a point of departure, this paper attends to another voice of American philosophy—that of Henry D. Thoreau, as revived by Stanley Cavell. I try to read Cavell's ‘Walden in Tokyo' as an exemplification of his ordinary language philosophy in its cross-cultural dimensions. Cavell's discussion invites the reader to reconsider what we mean by ‘understanding' ‘different' ‘cultures'. My hope is to show in the process the point of the title of Cavell's essay. Among the various entry points to cultural and cross-cultural matters I consider, a particular focus is given to Cavell’s idea of philosophy as translation. As a broader implication of this, I draw out an alternative possibility of becoming cosmopolitan: what happens in the very moment of encountering the untranslatable provides us with an occasion for the transfiguration of our lives. We cannot encounter different cultures as other cultures if we remain fixed within expectations of reciprocal interaction. The teaching of Walden is always indirect, and its purpose is not to moralize about the virtues of acknowledging differences and mutual understanding. This has implications for the educati

title: Cultural melancholy and moral perfectionism in Robles Godoy’s The Green Wall
text_snippet: Cultural melancholy and moral perfectionism in Robles Godoy’s The Green Wall Abstract This article examines Armando Robles Godoy’s 1969 Peruvian film La muralla verde (The Green Wall) through the philosophical lens of Stanley Cavell, particularly his concepts of scepticism, acknowledgement, and moral perfectionism. The film’s depiction of a family seeking renewal in the jungle, only to be devastated by tragedy, stages an encounter with the limits of human mastery over nature, the fragility of social bonds, and the inevitability of grief. Rather than offering nostalgia for a lost harmony or a straightforward political denunciation, The Green Wall invites a sustained engagement with the ethical demands of acknowledgement—of others, of the environment, and of the limits of one’s own knowledge. Read against the background of Latin America’s colonial legacy, Cavell’s Emersonian call to the ordinary provides a counterpoint to the region’s inherited scepticism and its persistent ‘cultural melancholy’, marked by the tension between cosmopolitan ideals and autochthonous realities. In this light, Robles Godoy’s film can be seen not only as a reflection of Perú’s fractured history but also as an instance of cinema’s philosophical power: its capacity to reawaken democr

title: Veena Das interviewed by Paul Standish
text_snippet: Veena Das interviewed by Paul Standish Abstract Veena Das is Professor Emerita in anthropology at Johns Hopkins University. She is the recipient of honorary doctorates from several universities and numerous other prestigious awards, including the John Simon Guggenheim Fellowship awarded in 2009. She taught at the Delhi School of Economics for more than thirty years and at the New School before she joined Johns Hopkins University in 2000. She is a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and in 2019 was elected a Corresponding Fellow of the British Academy. Her research interests range across anthropology, philosophy, and literature. She is particularly interested in how the textures and contours of everyday life can be rendered, with the everyday and the event conjoined in the making of the ordinary and the critical. She is known particularly for her work on childhood, suffering, and violence, health and disease, and urban transformations. Her life and career have been influenced from early on by her reading of Wittgenstein and of classical Sanskrit texts. She has participated closely in bringing Stanley Cavell’s philosophy to bear on anthropological modes of enquiry and in nourishing the anthropological tone

title: Walden in Tokyo
text_snippet: Walden in Tokyo Abstract Stanley Cavell wrote this article on the occasion of the first publication of one of his books in Japanese. The Senses of Walden, translated by Naoko Saito, was published by Hosei University Press in 2005. The paper was subsequently presented at two colloquia held at Harvard University in the development of the present collection. The article recalls aspects of the writing of his book on Walden, interweaving these with reflections on the relationship in philosophy between East and West and questions of mutual understanding. The discussion focuses particularly on Heidegger’s ‘A Dialogue on Language between a Japanese and an Inquirer’ and on questions of culture, high and low. Many of the articles that follow in this special issue, ‘Walden in Tokyo: Stanley Cavell and the Thought of Other Cultures’, pick up topics and themes that are addressed in Cavell’s discussion.

title: Stanley Cavell in Caracas: Excerpts from seminars and conversations with Victor J. Krebs and Maria Elena Ramos
text_snippet: Stanley Cavell in Caracas: Excerpts from seminars and conversations with Victor J. Krebs and Maria Elena Ramos Abstract We present here excerpts from seminars, interviews, and conversations with Stanley Cavell during the time of his visit to Caracas in 1998. This material comprises Cavell’s responses to questions raised at the seminar, extracts from an interview with Maria Elena Ramos and Victor Krebs, and a subsequent letter they received from Cavell in response to further questions. Krebs’ introduction to the collection sets the scene for Cavell’s visit and sketches some reasons for the relevance of Cavell’s philosophy to Latin America and the nature of its reception there.

title: Cavell and the thought of other cultures: an introduction
text_snippet: Cavell and the thought of other cultures: an introduction Abstract This introduction sets the scene for the articles and interviews that follow by providing an account of themes and approaches in the work of Stanley Cavell that relate especially to the idea of other cultures. The ‘thought of other cultures' is a richly ambiguous expression. It refers most obviously to the thinking and cultural products of different cultures. But, it also calls into question in what sense the words ‘other' and ‘culture' are to be taken, as well as how far the relationship to other cultures reaches back into the ways that one's ‘home' culture, and indeed one's subjectivity, are to be understood. The account relates these matters both to Cavell's interest, throughout his writings, in education and to his more particular arguments regarding scepticism. The importance of his readings of Emerson, Thoreau, and Wittgenstein are evident in the work of our contributors, and indeed in his own lead essay to this collection, ‘Walden in Tokyo’. In pondering these matters, the idea of the ordinary recurs. Footnotes provide a guide to the rich range of the contributions that ensue.

title: The spiralling life of Sámi children: whirls of organism and Indigenous relational philosophies
text_snippet: The spiralling life of Sámi children: whirls of organism and Indigenous relational philosophies Abstract The article investigates how meaning unfolds in the movements and entanglements of children, of teachers, of researchers, of animals, and of land—emerging in lived relations of meaning and otherness through the concrete whirls, swirls, and spirals of living together. It is grounded in an ethnographic narrative of an occasion when children from a Sámi Early Childhood Centre visited a reindeer gathering place in the mountains. With this narrative the article explores Stanley Cavell’s reading of Ludwig Wittgenstein’s notion of forms of life as ‘whirls of organism’, alongside anthropologist Tim Ingold’s reference to such whirls. The whirl and the spiral are read as movements of relationality, as emphasized by Indigenous scholars such as Jo-Ann Archibald, Margaret Kovach, Rauna Kuokkanen, Shawn Wilson, and the Sámi poet Inga Ravna Eira. Through this discussion the article extends some of Cavell’s writings about otherness in terms of what relations between we, I, and you can mean when land is regarded as a first form of relation. title: Stanley Cavell interviewed by Naoko Saito
text_snippet: Stanley Cavell interviewed by Naoko Saito Abstract In this interview with Naoko Saito, Stanley Cavell responds to questions about how he became interested in Wittgenstein and his sense of Wittgenstein’s fundamental importance for the question of what philosophy is or can be. Wittgenstein’s difference from Dewey and pragmatism is discussed in relation to the tone of philosophy, including possibilities of its not being characterized by polemical argument or geared towards problem-solving. This develops into a series of reflections on Emerson and Thoreau, as Cavell pursues these in The Senses of Walden. Similarly, some apparent similarities with, though in fact important differences from, Heidegger are considered, especially regarding the returning of philosophy to the ordinary and the finding of the ‘sublime in the pedestrian’. The conversation then turns to Wittgenstein’s alleged behaviourism: Cavell clarifies what he takes Wittgenstein to be opposing, and what endorsing, in conceptions of mind. title: The ordinary translated: towards a Wittgensteinian philosophy of culture
text_snippet: The ordinary translated: towards a Wittgensteinian philosophy of culture Abstract This article explores the relationship between the philosophy of ordinary language, American transcendentalism, and the anthropology of the ordinary, situating them within a broader reflection on expression and culture. Drawing on Wittgenstein, Cavell, and Das, it argues that the ordinary is neither synonymous with the common nor reducible to shared beliefs or dispositions; rather, it is constituted by our capacity for mutual understanding within language as a life form. Ordinary language philosophy reveals the vulnerability of expression and its dependence on the life form that gives words meaning. Cavell’s ‘sceptical’ reading of Wittgenstein uncovers the fragility of our linguistic and moral agreements, while his return to Emerson and Thoreau reframes American philosophy as a response to scepticism through the rediscovery of the everyday. Emerson’s and Thoreau’s calls to attend to the familiar, the low, and the everyday mark the beginnings of an American philosophy grounded in the democratization of perception and expression. title: Nothing to report: moral and pedagogical reflections from a voyage into engineering curricula for Sustainable Development Goals
text_snippet: Nothing to report: moral and pedagogical reflections from a voyage into engineering curricula for Sustainable Development Goals Abstract This essay chronicles the intellectual voyage of an ordinary language philosopher within a European Union-funded project (A-STEP 2030) using quantitative social science methods to define sustainability competencies for engineering education. Thinking through the standard ‘lit review’ and expert-validation procedures, it explores the philosophical and pedagogical perplexities emergent from arrogating a right to claim to know how to educate coming generations in order to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. Drawing on thinkers like Cavell, Wittgenstein, Emerson, and Thoreau, it raises sceptical questions regarding the ways in which our intellectual tools may limit our capacity to shape a future different from our present, about the arrogance of expertise, and even about the possible limits of ordinary language as it is ordinarily practised to address the deep problems raised by the current polycrisis. title: Who is my neighbour? Scepticism and the claims of alterity
text_snippet: Who is my neighbour? Scepticism and the claims of alterity Abstract This article begins with the question put by the teacher of the law to Jesus about the limits of obligation to the stranger and, hence, the extent of neighbourhood. It relates this to the ways in which ideas of alterity are manifested in the language of multiculturalism, now a somewhat tarnished term, and cultural diversity, which has gained greater currency though far from universal respect. It considers the inflation of language that occurs where ‘other’ is capitalized and acknowledges the indirect influence of Emmanuel Levinas in this. This has contributed to what I take to be a scepticist distortion of Levinas, especially in the conceptualization of the cultural other. In light of this reservation, attention is turned to the more nuanced account of such a relation that is to be found in the work of Stanley Cavell, especially in his reading of Thoreau’s Walden. Particular attention is given to Cavell’s late essay ‘Walden in Tokyo’, in which a contrast is drawn between Thoreau’s reception of East Asian influences and Heidegger’s encounter with Japanese thought. title: The concept of reflection in the work of John Dewey
text_snippet: The concept of reflection in the work of John Dewey Abstract John Dewey’s writings on thought form the groundwork for most modern conceptions of reflection. By revisiting these writings, this article provides an examination of his view of reflection, and its connection to his broader philosophy of cultural naturalism. Aimed at making Dewey’s ideas accessible to a new audience, the article first introduces key concepts from Dewey’s philosophy of cultural naturalism as they pertain to reflection. It then explores Dewey’s understanding of the reflective process and identifies obstacles which may lead to a premature conclusion. The article further explains how reflective practices can be nurtured within educational settings, offering a visual model of facilitated reflection. Finally, the article concludes by considering the relevance of Dewey’s insights for contemporary discussions of cognition, underscoring their enduring impact and practical applicability.

title: Language games in conversation: the ordinary as a site of criticism
text_snippet: Language games in conversation: the ordinary as a site of criticism Abstract Wittgenstein and Cavell show that the ordinary is not reducible to social conventions but is rooted in the vertical dimension of forms of life, revealed in the most common and apparently manifest gestures and expressions. Cavell’s reading of Fred Astaire’s dance in Vincente Minnelli’s The Band Wagon offers a vivid example: against a political backdrop, the routine discloses a future that may be barred yet emerges as an internal possibility. Inheriting and criticizing culture here occur in the motions and expressions of the body, revealed as a space where acknowledgement and transformation are possible, even if only as a momentary achievement. Such criticism arises from within, responding to what is missed or concealed in shared life and seeking untaken possibilities embedded in it.

title: Truthiness versus educational goods: three examples from the post-truth era
text_snippet: Truthiness versus educational goods: three examples from the post-truth era Abstract This article applies the Educational Goods Framework (EGF) developed by Harry Brighouse, Helen F. Ladd, Susanna Loeb, and Adam Swift to educational interventions addressing the challenges of the post-truth era. The term ‘post-truth’ refers to a context where emotional appeals and personal beliefs overshadow objective facts in shaping public opinion and political debate. A related concept, truthiness, describes the appearance of truth without necessarily being true. The prevalence of disinformation and conspiracy theories, particularly on the Internet and social media, exemplifies this phenomenon. The article uses the EGF’s powerful conceptual tools to sketch out the phenomenon of truthiness and its relationship to schools and education. Following this, the article explores three educational interventions to build resilience against truthiness: (1) enhancing standard educational goods, (2) implementing information literacy programmes, and (3) addressing truthiness directly in the classroom through discussions on controversial topics, as proposed by Glenn Bezalel. title: AI, the conflicted university, and the classroom
text_snippet: AI, the conflicted university, and the classroom Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has made it possible for students to complete writing assignments without undergoing the rigorous research, thinking, essay construction, and revision traditionally associated with college-level writing. What is more, this technology has made violations of academic honour policies nearly impossible to reliably demonstrate, leaving the policies largely unenforceable. This article explores the impact of generative AI within higher education by contextualizing its introduction within the neoliberal university. To clarify what is at stake, the article appeals to Alasdair MacIntyre's distinction between goods that are intrinsic to a social practice, internal goods, and those that are received as a reward for engaging in the practice, or external goods. When applied to the contemporary educational context, MacIntyre's distinction works to highlight the ways neoliberal higher education sacrifices the goods internal to academic practices in pursuing external goods such as money and recognition.
