title: Educational goods: flourishing, trade-offs and perfectionism
text_snippet: Educational goods: flourishing, trade-offs and perfectionism Abstract This article argues that the educational goods framework developed by Brighouse, Ladd, Loeb, and Swift (BLLS) is more useful to educational decision makers when it is underpinned by a perfectionist approach without neutralist constraints. This is because when policymakers are to make trade-offs between the relevant flourishing-related capacities, some value trade-offs will be necessary between the educational goods because the conditions which are required to develop some of the capacities may compete in nature. I argue that, even though the educational goods and relevant capacities can be supported by appealing to either a plausible perfectionist conception of political morality or a plausible anti-perfectionist account, ultimately, this is only of theoretical significance. This is because anti-perfectionist considerations are unhelpful in informing decision makers as to how to operationalize the trade-offs in question. Because of this, the article concludes that the framework becomes much easier to operationalize when it is underpinned by a perfectionist understanding of human flourishing.

title: Envisioning online learning spaces in higher education as spaces of radical openness: a philosophical scaffold for design
text_snippet: Envisioning online learning spaces in higher education as spaces of radical openness: a philosophical scaffold for design Abstract A persistent challenge in educational technology design is the construction of online environments. How might these spaces be constructed so that, rather than reinforcing socially entrenched but distorted norms and institutional interests, they are spaces of radical openness, centring the voices of all students while preparing them to create social change? This article takes up this challenge by exploring how postphenomenology, assemblage theory, and feminist technoscience could serve as philosophical scaffolding for such design. Postphenomenology contributes to seeing how learning spaces can be spaces of radical openness by fostering embodied vulnerability, allowing students and instructors to see one another as persons, and to be in-humanity-with one another. Assemblage theory calls attention to the materiality of online environments, how these spaces are socially situated and shaped by power relations, letting students see these forces and ask how distortive ones might be overcome. title: Risking human dignity? Reflections on transhumanist understandings of education
text_snippet: Risking human dignity? Reflections on transhumanist understandings of education Abstract Transhumanists profess a commitment to the betterment of humanity by transcending human nature and taking control of evolution through scientific interventions that realize humanity’s inherent potentialities. The authors question transhumanist assumptions vis-à-vis education and the understanding of the person, with specific reference to leading metahumanist Stefan Sorgner. He argues that, according to the theory of evolution, it is no longer possible to claim that only humans count as persons. He maintains that personhood depends on morally relevant capacities and views education as structurally analogous to genetic enhancement. This rejects the Judeo-Christian and humanistic understanding that only humans in this connection count as persons. Sorgner opposes the humanist ontology, eschewing the Kantian moral injunction to never treat a person solely as a means. This principle, which rests on the distinction between persons and things, has safeguarded human dignity. title: Towards a conceptualization of computational thinking as situated
text_snippet: Towards a conceptualization of computational thinking as situated Abstract Computational thinking (CT) is currently being introduced into non-computer science disciplines at all educational levels. Many who have written on or implemented CT in educational contexts claim that CT is a universally applicable set of general problem-solving skills. I challenge this claim by discussing how CT is used in practice within everyday contexts and in learning within different disciplines. I propose an alternative conceptualization of CT as being socially and disciplinarily situated and transforming across these contexts. I discuss the significance of a situated conceptualization of CT for educational and research practices, highlighting through example cases the risks that choosing an inadequate conceptualization of CT has for disciplinary learning. These risks include concentrating student learning time on neither meeting discipline-specific learning objectives nor on developing computer science skills, but on an artificial intermediary. title: A Ricœurian approach to education: articulating the ‘will-to-live-together’ and ‘conflictual consensus’ in democratic societies
text_snippet: A Ricœurian approach to education: articulating the ‘will-to-live-together’ and ‘conflictual consensus’ in democratic societies Abstract This article explores the potential of Paul Ricœur’s political philosophy for conceptualizing education in democratic societies. While Ricœur did not develop a systematic philosophy of education, his work offers rich resources for reimagining education’s role in fostering democratic citizenship. By integrating Ricœur’s scattered reflections on education into his broader political philosophy, this article proposes an educational approach centred on cultivating the ‘will-to-live-together’ through ‘conflictual consensus’. It argues that these concepts provide a compelling framework for managing societal pluralism and developing democratic competencies. The article concludes by offering practical suggestions to implement this educational vision.

title: Crises of acknowledgement: oblique actions and ominous verbs
text_snippet: Crises of acknowledgement: oblique actions and ominous verbs Abstract Acknowledging other human beings, especially when they speak a language foreign to us, comport themselves in ways we find illegible, makes manifest just how difficult the work of acknowledgement is. But the pitfalls in devoting oneself to such work are of a piece with those woven into the fabric of acknowledging others with whom we share a culture. The author of this article explores the work of acknowledgement, in light of both its Wittgensteinian inspiration and some surprising implications of paying close attention to several important claims made by J. L. Austin in ‘A Plea for Excuses’. The ‘natural economy of language’ might work against acknowledging our complicity in nothing less than the annihilation of others, especially those who speak, act, look, and in respects appear to be so different from ourselves. While our relationship to others tends to be, as Emerson noted, ‘oblique and casual’, killing in even a figurative sense is, as Austin suggested, ‘a verb of omen’. Arguably, oblique actions have more to do with ominous verbs than we appreciate—or tend to acknowledge. Such, at least, is what the author tries to render plausible.

title: Aristotle on the role of cross-generational friendship in young adult moral development
text_snippet: Aristotle on the role of cross-generational friendship in young adult moral development Abstract Building on recent philosophical scholarship in the overlapping domains of friendship and moral development, this article argues in favour of Aristotelian character friendship as a special mode of interpersonal relationship that uniquely facilitates moral development by relaxing the distinction between friend, mentor, and role model. Taking an interdisciplinary approach that integrates ideas from human development and philosophy, this article advances a series of interlocking arguments, supported by textual exegesis, which yields a conclusion with significant implications for the ongoing discussion about the role of friendship in moral development. The article challenges certain assumptions about the nature of Aristotelian character friendship present in the current literature by situating Aristotle's account of friendship in its broader cultural and historical context. It then develops an alternative picture of Aristotelian character friendship wherein friendships of the kind that promote moral development consist primarily of partnerships between younger and older men.

title: The ordinary in Cavell, Zen, and Nishida: with reference to the quotidian in French, Japanese, and American cinema
text_snippet: The ordinary in Cavell, Zen, and Nishida: with reference to the quotidian in French, Japanese, and American cinema Abstract This article discusses Stanley Cavell's view of Emerson, Thoreau, and American transcendentalism in relation to Asian philosophy, including aspects of Indian and Japanese thought. Especially I refer to Cavell's essay ‘Walden in Tokyo’ as a springboard to analyse his key problem of countering scepticism by return to the ordinary as extraordinary in American transcendentalism as related to Zen and the modern Japanese philosophy of Nishida Kitarō. Furthermore, I develop Cavell's thematization of ‘the ordinary’ in critical response to what has come to be known in the Franco-German tradition as ‘everyday life cultural studies’, which proclaims le quotidien or ‘the quotidian’ to be the fundamental category of human existence, including its creative expression in French art, literature, and film. This European tradition of everyday life cultural theory also makes the claim that while ‘the quotidian’ has been discovered and explored by the French, it has not yet been grasped by American thought and culture. title: Exploring the logic of (modern) education: a general educational perspective
text_snippet: Exploring the logic of (modern) education: a general educational perspective Abstract Contrary to a dominant, instrumental way of thinking about education, there has been a growing focus in recent years on the problem of the intrinsic logic of education. This article argues that the German-speaking tradition of General Education (Allgemeine Pädagogik) provides valuable insights for critically engaging with recent attempts to conceptualize this logic. Against this background, the article highlights key challenges which, if addressed, could advance the enquiry into educational questions about education. The first challenge concerns the plurality of theoretical perspectives on the logic of education. The article contends that this plurality does not undermine General Education but calls for explicit reflection on one’s presuppositions and critical engagement with existing positions. The second challenge lies in distinguishing between the logic of education in general and the logic of modern education in particular. title: Teaching progress? On the role of history in democratic education
text_snippet: Teaching progress? On the role of history in democratic education Abstract A central aim of democratic education is enabling students to critically engage with past, present, and future sociopolitical struggles. Doing justice to this temporal dimension requires providing an epistemically adequate and normatively apt understanding of history, including the directive teaching of criteria for moral-political progress and regression. This contribution defends these claims in three steps. First, it introduces an educational framework for teaching for and about progress. Second, it outlines a deliberative and liberal-perfectionist conception of moral-political progress, distinguishing it from classical and contemporary alternatives. Third, drawing on the work of Theodor W. Adorno and Jürgen Habermas, it conceptualizes democratic education as a historically situated normative learning process that combines two core features. The first feature involves the acknowledgement of past wrongs and injustices and of structural continuities that connect the past with the present.
